transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
President Trump is using what's known as a pocket rescission to cancel nearly $1 billion
in federal funding approved by Congress, NPR's Ava Pukach reports.
The timing of the move just days before the fiscal year ends means Congress won't likely
have time to address the cuts before they go into effect.
The White House says the cuts focus on "wasteful and harmful government spending."
A majority of the cuts are to programs at the Department of Health and Human Services.
Others target education programs for migrant students, and a Department of Justice agency
focused on reducing racial tensions.
The pocket rescission drew bipartisan congressional backlash, including from Republican Senator
Susan Collins of Maine, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, who said she would
work with her colleagues to address "these illegal actions."
Ava Pukach, NPR News.
Former Kennedy Center employees say several months ago the institution's leadership canceled
a plan to repair significant leaks in the main building.
The center's board now says those leaks were so urgent that the complex had to close immediately.
NPR's Anastasia C. Lucas has more.
In a letter sent to two congressional committees, the whistleblowers say the center's current
executive director, Matt Floga, had secured $9.3 million to replace and repair water leaks
in the center's roof and soffits.
Those repairs were approved in August 2025, according to supplemental documents also filed
with Congress.
But this April, the whistleblowers say Floga canceled the repair plan four months before
the Kennedy Center's board approved shutting the arts complex immediately.
They also say some of the waterproofing funds were diverted for repainting exterior columns
and other cosmetic changes President Trump desired.
The Kennedy Center did not respond immediately to NPR's request for comment.
Anastasia C. Lucas, NPR News.
A powerful storm system continues to batter the Northeast Coast's flooding streets and
homes and knocking out power to more than 100,000 customers.
The nor'easter is also disrupting flights at several airports in the region.
National Weather Service meteorologist Frank Pereira says the storm is currently stalled
off the coast of New Jersey.
"The system itself is centered off the New Jersey, the Long Island coast, and it's going
to continue to sit there for the next day or so, just kind of drifting in the area.
And as it does, it will continue to bring coastal impacts, non-settle weather, across
portions of the mid-Atlantic to New England through the remainder of the weekend."
On Cape Cod, resident Sue Mastria says a tree came down on her home while she was asleep.
"I was asleep at 3 a.m. all of a sudden I heard 'Boom!' and I said, 'It's the tree.'"
Forecasters say several inches of rain could fall before the storm moves out, adding to
the threat of coastal flooding.
This is NPR.
Hurricane Noloe is moving west south of Hawaii after bringing heavy rain to the Big Island.
The National Weather Service says the threat of flooding is ease, but strong winds will
continue across the islands today.
High wind warnings remain in effect for parts of Maui and the Big Island.
Another east in the Pacific, Hurricane Polo is threatening Mexico's Baja California
Peninsula.
Forecasters expected to make landfall Monday as a weaker storm.
Polo is also sending dangerous surf towards southern California, where officials are warning
of rip currents and coastal flooding.
President Trump made a trip to Knoxville, Tennessee to watch No. 1-ranked Texas take
on the Tennessee volunteers yesterday.
Reagan Jones from member station WOT reports.
President Trump's attendance generated mixed feelings from fans, but even with the added
security protocols, the energy was undeniable.
Adam Husseini graduated from the University of Tennessee and has attended several games
over the years.
But he said the atmosphere here is extra special.
"Unlike anything I've ever seen, it is another level to what we usually see."
Ball's fan Jeremy Littrell said he wouldn't be surprised if the visit had a political
motive.
But either way, he's happy to see football bringing people together.
"This is college football and I don't care who you voted for or what politics affiliation
you're with, it's goal balls, baby."
The game is the first match-up between the two UTs in over half a century.
For NPR News, I'm Reagan Jones in Knoxville.
This is NPR News in Washington.
